david-attenborough-a-life-on-our-planet.summary: David Attenborough's 'witness statement' tracing how wild nature has declined over his lifetime as human population and CO2 rose. It ends with a solutions vision built around rewilding the world.
takeaways: Wild places shrank from about two-thirds to about one-third of the land in his lifetime
Biodiversity loss and climate change are linked crises
Rewilding land and sea can restore stability
Raising living standards, eating more plants and renewables are core fixes

cards.q: Where does the film open, as a symbol of human-caused abandonment?
cards.a: The abandoned city of Pripyat near Chernobyl
cards.explain: The deserted town near Chernobyl frames the warning that human mistakes can make places uninhabitable.
wrong: A burning forest in the Amazon

cards.q: What does Attenborough call the film?
cards.a: His 'witness statement' for the natural world
cards.explain: He frames it as first-hand testimony of the decline he has seen across decades of filmmaking.
wrong: A manifesto for a political party
A history of the BBC Natural History Unit

cards.q: Roughly how has remaining wilderness changed over his lifetime, per the film?
cards.a: From about two-thirds of land to about one-third
cards.explain: The film tracks world population, atmospheric CO2 and remaining wilderness at points in his life to show the trend.
wrong: From about one-third of land to about one-half
Stayed roughly constant at about one-half
From nearly all land to under five percent

cards.q: Why does the film stress the Holocene?
cards.a: Its stable climate allowed agriculture and civilization to flourish
cards.explain: The roughly 10,000-year Holocene was unusually stable; the film warns human activity is pushing Earth out of it.
wrong: It was the era when dinosaurs went extinct
It was a period of rapid ice-age cycles
It is when fossil fuels first formed

cards.q: What ocean solution does the film highlight?
cards.a: No-fishing zones that let fish stocks recover
cards.explain: Marine protected areas let populations rebuild and spill over into fished areas, as with the Palau example.
wrong: Farming fish in floating offshore cages
Adding iron to the ocean to grow plankton
Banning all shipping on the high seas

cards.q: How does the film suggest slowing population growth?
cards.a: Raising living standards, healthcare and education, especially for girls
cards.explain: Where people are healthier, wealthier and better educated, family sizes fall and population peaks sooner.
wrong: Mandatory limits on children per family
Moving people to new cities on other continents

breaking-boundaries-the-science-of-our-p.summary: Scientist Johan Rockstrom, with narration by David Attenborough, explains the planetary boundaries framework. It shows which Earth-system limits humanity has already crossed and what a 'safe operating space' requires.
takeaways: There are nine planetary boundaries
Several, including climate and biodiversity, are already crossed
The ozone layer shows a boundary can be pulled back
Staying near Holocene conditions keeps Earth resilient

cards.q: Which scientist presents the planetary boundaries in the film?
cards.a: Johan Rockstrom
cards.explain: Rockstrom led the team that proposed the planetary boundaries framework in 2009 at the Stockholm Resilience Centre.

cards.q: How many planetary boundaries does the framework define?
cards.a: Nine
cards.explain: They include climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater, biogeochemical flows, ozone, aerosols, ocean acidification and novel entities.

cards.q: What does the 'safe operating space' mean?
cards.a: The zone within the boundaries where Earth stays stable for humanity
cards.explain: Staying inside the boundaries keeps the planet close to the stable Holocene-like conditions civilization depends on.
wrong: The area of land safe from sea-level rise
The emissions budget for a single country
The orbit range of climate satellites

cards.q: Which boundary is presented as a success story of pulling back?
cards.a: Stratospheric ozone, thanks to the Montreal Protocol
cards.explain: Phasing out CFCs under the 1987 Montreal Protocol is letting the ozone layer recover.
wrong: Climate change, thanks to the Kyoto Protocol

cards.q: At the time of the film, how many boundaries were said to be crossed?
cards.a: Four, including climate change and biodiversity loss
cards.explain: The film cites climate, biodiversity, land-use change and nitrogen/phosphorus flows; a 2023 update said six were crossed.
wrong: None yet, but all are close

cards.q: Why are tipping points such as the Greenland ice sheet and Amazon a concern?
cards.a: Crossing them can trigger self-reinforcing, hard-to-reverse change
cards.explain: Once past a threshold, feedbacks can keep change going even if pressure is reduced.
wrong: They only matter for local weather
They reverse quickly once emissions stop
They cool the planet as they change

before-the-flood.summary: Leonardo DiCaprio, as a UN Messenger of Peace on climate, travels the world meeting scientists, leaders and affected communities. It covers impacts, drivers like deforestation and beef, and solutions such as carbon pricing and clean energy.
takeaways: Climate impacts are already visible from the Arctic to Miami
Deforestation for palm oil is a major emissions source
Diet, especially beef, matters for emissions
A price on carbon is a key policy lever

cards.q: What does the title 'Before the Flood' refer to?
cards.a: A panel of Bosch's painting 'The Garden of Earthly Delights'
cards.explain: The painting, which hung over DiCaprio's crib, shows paradise turning to ruin - a metaphor for climate change.
wrong: The biblical story of Noah's Ark only
A 2005 hurricane that flooded New Orleans
A UN report on sea-level rise

cards.q: What does the film show happening to Indonesian rainforests?
cards.a: Burned and cleared for palm oil plantations
cards.explain: Clearing and burning forests and peatlands releases large amounts of carbon and destroys wildlife habitat.

cards.q: What point is raised in India about responsibility?
cards.a: Rich countries' high per-capita consumption versus energy access needs
cards.explain: The film highlights that hundreds of millions lack reliable power while wealthy nations consume far more per person.
wrong: India alone must cut emissions first
Poor countries emit most per person
Energy access does not affect emissions

cards.q: Why does the film single out beef?
cards.a: Cattle need lots of land and emit methane
cards.explain: Beef is far more land- and emissions-intensive than most foods, so dietary shifts can cut emissions.
wrong: Beef farming absorbs more CO2 than it emits
Cattle are mostly raised on solar-powered farms
Beef has lower emissions than beans

cards.q: What policy solution do economists in the film emphasize?
cards.a: A tax or price on carbon emissions
cards.explain: Pricing carbon makes polluters pay for damage and shifts markets toward clean options.

cards.q: What does the film show in Miami?
cards.a: Streets flooding at high tide as seas rise
cards.explain: Sea-level rise is causing 'sunny day' flooding, forcing costly road raising and pumps.

an-inconvenient-sequel-truth-to-power.summary: A decade after An Inconvenient Truth, Al Gore trains climate leaders and works behind the scenes at the 2015 Paris talks. The film highlights worsening impacts alongside the rapid rise and falling cost of solar and wind.
takeaways: Gore trains volunteer climate communicators worldwide
Solar and wind costs have fallen dramatically
Clean energy can win on economics, even in conservative places
The Paris Agreement aims for well below 2C

cards.q: What major activity of Al Gore does the film follow?
cards.a: Training climate leaders through the Climate Reality Project
cards.explain: Gore runs trainings that teach volunteers to give climate presentations in their own communities.

cards.q: Why did Georgetown, Texas move to 100% renewable power in the film?
cards.a: Its Republican mayor saw lower, stable prices
cards.explain: The city's choice was driven by long-term price certainty from wind and solar contracts, not ideology.
wrong: A federal mandate forced the change
It lost access to all natural gas
A climate activist group bought the utility

cards.q: What was a key sticking point with India at the Paris talks?
cards.a: Access to solar technology and financing
cards.explain: India needed affordable clean-energy tech and finance; Gore helped broker solar technology access.
wrong: India demanded a ban on coal worldwide
India refused to attend the conference

cards.q: Which earlier prediction does the film say came true in 2012?
cards.a: Storm surge flooding the World Trade Center memorial site
cards.explain: Hurricane Sandy flooded lower Manhattan, including the 9/11 site Gore had warned about in the first film.

cards.q: What trend in clean energy does the film celebrate?
cards.a: Rapidly falling costs and rising deployment of solar and wind
cards.explain: Solar and wind became competitive with fossil power, making the transition economically attractive.

cards.q: What temperature goal came out of the Paris Agreement?
cards.a: Well below 2C, pursuing 1.5C
cards.explain: Parties agreed to hold warming well below 2C above pre-industrial and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5C.

2040.summary: Director Damon Gameau imagines the world his daughter could grow up in by 2040 if solutions that already exist today were fully scaled. It covers decentralized energy, transport, regenerative farming, ocean solutions and empowering women.
takeaways: Only solutions available today are used
Rooftop solar microgrids can share power peer to peer
Shared electric transport can free up city space
Regenerative farming and seaweed can draw down carbon

cards.q: What rule does the film set for imagining 2040?
cards.a: Only use solutions that already exist today
cards.explain: Gameau avoids speculative tech, showing what could happen by scaling current solutions.

cards.q: What framing device does the director use?
cards.a: A visual letter to his young daughter
cards.explain: The film is structured as a message to his daughter about the future she could inherit.
wrong: A courtroom trial of oil companies
A diary written by a future robot

cards.q: What energy model does the film show from Bangladesh?
cards.a: Home solar microgrids with peer-to-peer power trading
cards.explain: Households with small solar systems trade surplus electricity with neighbors, bringing power without a central grid.
wrong: Large coal plants feeding a national grid
Offshore wind farms owned by the state

cards.q: How does the film imagine transport changing?
cards.a: Shared, electric, autonomous vehicles reducing car ownership
cards.explain: Fewer private cars frees streets and parking for people and green space.
wrong: Everyone owning two private gasoline cars

cards.q: What ocean solution is featured?
cards.a: Marine permaculture: seaweed or kelp platforms
cards.explain: Growing seaweed can provide food and habitat and absorb carbon while restoring ocean ecosystems.

cards.q: Which social solution does the film present as a climate solution?
cards.a: Educating girls and empowering women
cards.explain: Education and access to family planning improve lives and lower population growth, a solution also ranked by Project Drawdown.
wrong: Lowering the voting age to twelve

kiss-the-ground.summary: Narrated by Woody Harrelson, the film argues that regenerative agriculture can rebuild soil health and pull carbon from the air into the ground. It covers no-till, cover crops, grazing and composting.
takeaways: Healthy soil can store carbon drawn down by plants
Tillage and bare soil release carbon and cause erosion
Cover crops and diverse rotations keep soil alive
The scale and permanence of soil carbon are debated

cards.q: What is the film's central claim about soil?
cards.a: Healthy soil can pull carbon from the atmosphere and store it
cards.explain: Plants capture CO2 by photosynthesis and pass carbon to soil through roots and microbes.
wrong: Soil emits no carbon under any conditions
Soil only matters for growing food
Soil carbon cannot be changed by farming

cards.q: Which conventional practice does the film say degrades soil carbon?
cards.a: Repeated tillage or plowing
cards.explain: Plowing breaks up soil structure, exposes organic matter to oxidation and increases erosion.

cards.q: Why does the film promote cover crops?
cards.a: They keep living roots and soil covered year-round
cards.explain: Cover crops reduce erosion, feed soil microbes and add organic matter between cash crops.
wrong: They replace the need for any harvest
They are sprayed to kill soil microbes
They keep fields bare and dry

cards.q: What historical disaster does the film use as a warning?
cards.a: The 1930s Dust Bowl
cards.explain: Plowed, drought-stricken Great Plains soils blew away, showing what happens when soil is degraded.

cards.q: Which idea in the film is notably contested by scientists?
cards.a: That managed grazing can reverse desertification at large scale
cards.explain: Holistic planned grazing is promoted in the film, but evidence for large-scale carbon gains is debated.

cards.q: What urban practice does the film highlight?
cards.a: City composting that returns food scraps to farms
cards.explain: San Francisco's program turns organic waste into compost that builds farm soil.
wrong: Burning food waste to make electricity

chasing-coral.summary: Divers, scientists and photographers use custom time-lapse cameras to document coral bleaching during a global mass bleaching event. It makes ocean warming visible and shows what is at stake for reefs.
takeaways: Bleaching is corals expelling algae under heat stress
Oceans absorb over 90% of excess heat
Repeated marine heatwaves are killing reefs worldwide
Reefs support a huge share of marine life

cards.q: What is coral bleaching?
cards.a: Corals expelling their symbiotic algae under heat stress
cards.explain: Without the algae that feed them and give color, corals turn white and can starve if heat persists.
wrong: Corals turning white from pollution dye
Corals growing too fast in warm water

cards.q: Is a bleached coral already dead?
cards.a: No, it can recover if temperatures drop soon enough
cards.explain: Bleaching is a stress response; prolonged or repeated heat leads to death.
wrong: Yes, and it cannot regrow anywhere nearby

cards.q: How did the team document bleaching?
cards.a: Custom underwater time-lapse cameras
cards.explain: Time-lapse imagery showed reefs bleaching and dying over weeks, making change visible.

cards.q: Roughly how much of the extra heat from global warming do oceans absorb?
cards.a: Over 90%
cards.explain: The ocean is the main heat sink of the climate system, driving marine heatwaves.

cards.q: Which major event does the film capture?
cards.a: The 2014-2017 global mass bleaching, including the Great Barrier Reef
cards.explain: In 2016 heat stress caused severe bleaching across large parts of the Great Barrier Reef.
wrong: An oil spill in the Caribbean

cards.q: Why do reefs matter so much for ocean life?
cards.a: They cover under 1% of the seafloor but host about a quarter of marine species
cards.explain: Reefs are biodiversity hotspots that also support fisheries, tourism and coastal protection.
wrong: They produce most of Earth's oxygen

ice-on-fire.summary: An HBO documentary produced and narrated by Leonardo DiCaprio that focuses on drawing carbon down, not just cutting emissions. It covers Arctic methane risks and solutions like direct air capture, biochar and ocean kelp.
takeaways: Cutting emissions is necessary but not sufficient
Thawing permafrost can release methane and CO2
Direct air capture, biochar and kelp can remove carbon
Methane is a powerful short-lived greenhouse gas

cards.q: What is the film's central message?
cards.a: We must cut emissions and also draw carbon down
cards.explain: The film argues that removal and natural sinks are needed alongside rapid emissions cuts.

cards.q: What Arctic risk does the film highlight?
cards.a: Thawing permafrost releasing methane and CO2
cards.explain: Warming permafrost can release stored carbon, creating a feedback that amplifies warming.
wrong: Arctic ice growing thicker each year

cards.q: What does direct air capture do?
cards.a: Uses machines and sorbents to pull CO2 from ambient air
cards.explain: Companies like Climeworks capture CO2 from air for storage or use; it remains costly and energy-intensive.
wrong: Filters smoke from factory chimneys only

cards.q: What is biochar?
cards.a: Charcoal made from biomass that stores carbon in soil
cards.explain: Heating biomass with little oxygen (pyrolysis) makes a stable carbon form that can last long in soil.

cards.q: Why does the film feature kelp and seaweed?
cards.a: Ocean forests absorb carbon and restore marine ecosystems
cards.explain: Kelp grows fast, takes up carbon and can reduce local acidity while supporting sea life.
wrong: They replace the need for fish
They block sunlight to cool the sea
They produce oil for fuel tanks

cards.q: Why is methane a priority in the film?
cards.a: It traps far more heat than CO2 over the short term
cards.explain: Methane is tens of times more potent than CO2 per ton, so cutting it slows near-term warming.
wrong: It lasts longer in the air than CO2
It is harmless in the atmosphere

climate-town.summary: A comedic YouTube channel by Rollie Williams explaining how energy, utilities, plastics and marketing shape climate outcomes. It focuses on systems, incentives and greenwashing rather than personal guilt.
takeaways: Utility profit models shape grid decisions
Most plastic is not actually recycled
Greenwashing hides real impacts
Policy and system design matter more than guilt

cards.q: How do US investor-owned utilities mainly earn profits?
cards.a: A regulated rate of return on capital they invest
cards.explain: Regulators let them earn a return on the 'rate base', so building more infrastructure tends to increase profit.
wrong: Selling as much fuel as possible to drivers

cards.q: Roughly what share of US plastic waste gets recycled?
cards.a: Less than 10%
cards.explain: Most plastic is landfilled or burned; many plastic types have no viable recycling market.

cards.q: What is greenwashing?
cards.a: Misleading claims that make something seem more eco-friendly
cards.explain: Vague labels, cherry-picked data and offset-based claims can hide real environmental impacts.
wrong: Painting buildings green to cool them

cards.q: Which oil company helped popularize the 'personal carbon footprint'?
cards.a: BP, through a mid-2000s ad campaign
cards.explain: Critics argue the campaign shifted focus from producers to individual consumers.
wrong: The UN, through the Kyoto Protocol

cards.q: How do parking minimums affect emissions?
cards.a: They force extra parking that encourages car dependence
cards.explain: Required off-street parking spreads cities out and makes driving the default.
wrong: They reduce driving by limiting cars
They require solar on every lot
They have no effect on land use

cards.q: What indoor air concern is raised about gas stoves?
cards.a: They emit pollutants like nitrogen dioxide indoors
cards.explain: Burning gas releases NO2 and other pollutants linked to respiratory problems, plus methane leaks.

technology-connections.summary: Alec Watson's channel explains how everyday appliances really work and use energy. Signature topics include heat pumps, why resistive heating is COP 1, and the refrigeration cycle.
takeaways: Resistive heating turns 1 unit of electricity into 1 unit of heat
Heat pumps move heat, delivering several units per unit of power
Refrigerators and air conditioners are heat pumps
Heat pumps keep working in cold weather, with lower efficiency

cards.q: Why is resistive electric heating said to have a COP of 1?
cards.a: Each unit of electricity becomes exactly one unit of heat
cards.explain: Resistive heaters are nearly 100% efficient at making heat, but cannot deliver more heat than the energy put in.
wrong: Half the electricity is lost as light
It makes three units of heat per unit

cards.q: How can a heat pump deliver more heat than the electricity it uses?
cards.a: It moves existing heat from outside rather than creating it
cards.explain: Electricity runs a compressor that transfers heat, so delivered heat exceeds input energy (COP above 1).
wrong: It burns a hidden fuel tank
It breaks the laws of thermodynamics

cards.q: In a heat pump cycle, what happens when refrigerant evaporates?
cards.a: It absorbs heat from its surroundings
cards.explain: The refrigerant boils at low pressure to absorb heat, then is compressed and condenses to release it elsewhere.
wrong: It releases heat into the room

cards.q: Can air-source heat pumps work when it is below freezing outside?
cards.a: Yes, though efficiency falls as it gets colder
cards.explain: Cold air still contains heat; modern cold-climate units work well below freezing at reduced COP.
wrong: Yes, and they get more efficient
Only if a gas furnace runs too

cards.q: Why is a refrigerator a heat pump?
cards.a: It moves heat out of the box and releases it into the room
cards.explain: The same refrigeration cycle that cools a fridge can heat a home when run the other way.
wrong: It destroys heat inside the box

cards.q: Why are heat pump water heaters more efficient than resistive tanks?
cards.a: They move heat from the air into the water
cards.explain: Moving heat lets them use roughly a third or less of the electricity of standard electric tanks.
wrong: They heat water only at night

engineering-with-rosie.summary: An engineer explains how renewables, storage and the power grid actually work. Topics include grid frequency and inertia, pumped hydro, hydrogen, offshore wind and transmission.
takeaways: Grid supply and demand must balance every second
Pumped hydro is the largest form of grid storage
Hydrogen loses much of its energy in conversion
High-voltage lines move power long distances efficiently

cards.q: Why must a power grid keep frequency near 50 or 60 Hz?
cards.a: Frequency drifts when supply and demand fall out of balance
cards.explain: Operators keep generation matched to load; large deviations can trip equipment and cause blackouts.
wrong: Frequency sets the price of power
Frequency controls the voltage of solar panels
Frequency is fixed by law and never moves

cards.q: What is grid inertia?
cards.a: Energy in spinning generators that resists sudden frequency changes
cards.explain: Heavy turbines slow frequency changes; inverter-based solar and wind need grid-forming controls to provide similar support.
wrong: The time it takes to build a power plant

cards.q: How does pumped hydro storage work?
cards.a: Pumps water uphill when power is cheap and releases it through turbines later
cards.explain: It is the largest form of grid-scale energy storage worldwide by capacity.

cards.q: Why is green hydrogen less efficient than using electricity directly?
cards.a: Much energy is lost in electrolysis, compression and conversion back
cards.explain: Round-trip power-to-hydrogen-to-power typically recovers well under half of the input energy.
wrong: Hydrogen produces more energy than it takes
Hydrogen cannot be stored at all

cards.q: Why build wind turbines offshore?
cards.a: Winds are stronger and steadier at sea
cards.explain: Offshore sites give higher capacity factors; floating platforms open deeper waters.
wrong: Seawater cools the blades for free
Waves generate most of the power

cards.q: Why use high-voltage DC lines for long-distance transmission?
cards.a: Lower losses over long distances and undersea cables
cards.explain: HVDC loses less energy over very long runs and allows linking unsynchronized grids.
wrong: They are cheaper for short distances

undecided-with-matt-ferrell.summary: Matt Ferrell reviews home solar, batteries and emerging energy technology with real-world numbers. Recurring topics include payback math, net metering, battery chemistries and bidirectional charging.
takeaways: Solar payback depends on rates, incentives and export policy
Weaker net metering favors adding batteries
LFP batteries trade energy density for safety and cycle life
EVs can power homes with bidirectional charging

cards.q: What mainly determines a home solar system's payback time?
cards.a: Electricity rates, upfront cost, incentives and export credit policy
cards.explain: High rates and good export credits shorten payback; weak incentives or low rates lengthen it.
wrong: The number of people in the house

cards.q: What is net metering?
cards.a: Credit for exported solar at or near the retail rate
cards.explain: Under net metering the meter effectively runs backward; net billing pays a lower export rate.
wrong: A fee for disconnecting from the grid
A cap on how much power you use

cards.q: Why do lower export credits (like California's NEM 3.0) favor home batteries?
cards.a: Storing solar for self-use is worth more than exporting it
cards.explain: When exports earn little, shifting solar to evening use avoids buying expensive grid power.
wrong: Batteries become free under the rules
Solar panels stop working at night

cards.q: How does LFP compare with NMC battery chemistry?
cards.a: Safer and longer-lasting but less energy dense
cards.explain: Lithium iron phosphate avoids nickel and cobalt and has more cycles, making it popular for homes and grid storage.
wrong: More energy dense but less safe

cards.q: What is the main appeal of sodium-ion batteries?
cards.a: Abundant, cheap materials, despite lower energy density
cards.explain: Sodium is plentiful, so these cells suit stationary storage and low-cost vehicles.
wrong: Highest energy density of any battery

cards.q: What does bidirectional (V2H/V2G) charging allow?
cards.a: An EV to send power back to a home or the grid
cards.explain: Vehicle-to-home can provide backup power; vehicle-to-grid can support the grid at peak times.
wrong: Charging two cars from one plug

volts.summary: David Roberts' deeply wonky interview show on clean energy, the grid and policy. Core themes include electrifying everything, grid bottlenecks like interconnection and transmission, and distributed energy.
takeaways: Electrifying end uses cuts energy waste and emissions
Interconnection queues and transmission are key bottlenecks
Virtual power plants can stand in for new plants
Existing grids can carry more with smarter tech

cards.q: Why does 'electrify everything' reduce emissions?
cards.a: Electric motors and heat pumps are efficient and the grid keeps getting cleaner
cards.explain: Replacing combustion in cars, buildings and industry cuts energy waste and lets clean power reach every use.
wrong: Electricity is always made from renewables
Burning fuel is more efficient than motors

cards.q: Why are interconnection queues a bottleneck?
cards.a: Projects wait years for grid studies and upgrade costs
cards.explain: Large backlogs of proposed generation and storage slow deployment, and many projects drop out.
wrong: There are too few solar panels to install
Utilities refuse to buy any power

cards.q: Why is new transmission so hard to build in the US?
cards.a: Multi-state permitting and fights over who pays
cards.explain: Long lines cross many jurisdictions and landowners, and cost allocation is contentious.
wrong: Wire is in short global supply
Transmission is banned by federal law

cards.q: What is a virtual power plant?
cards.a: Many distributed devices coordinated to act like a power plant
cards.explain: Aggregated batteries, thermostats, EV chargers and solar can supply or reduce demand on command.
wrong: A simulated power plant in software only
A plant run remotely by robots
A power plant on a ship

cards.q: What are grid-enhancing technologies and reconductoring?
cards.a: Ways to carry more power on existing lines
cards.explain: Dynamic line ratings, power-flow controls and advanced conductors expand capacity faster than new lines.
wrong: Building new coal plants near cities

shift-key.summary: Heatmap's weekly show with Robinson Meyer and Princeton modeler Jesse Jenkins on energy and climate policy. It focuses on energy-system modeling, US clean-energy tax credits and their 2025 rollback, and rising power demand.
takeaways: Energy models estimate how policy changes emissions and costs
The IRA drove clean energy mainly through tax credits
The 2025 law phases down wind and solar credits
Clean firm power lowers the cost of deep decarbonization

cards.q: What do energy-system models like Princeton's REPEAT project do?
cards.a: Estimate how policies change emissions, costs and the energy mix
cards.explain: Modeling simulates investment and operations to project outcomes under different policies.
wrong: Measure the weather in real time

cards.q: How did the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act mainly support clean energy?
cards.a: Long-term tax credits for clean power, EVs and manufacturing
cards.explain: It was the largest US climate law, largely built on production and investment tax credits.
wrong: A cap on all utility emissions

cards.q: Under the July 2025 US law, how must wind and solar qualify for credits?
cards.a: Begin construction by July 4, 2026, or be in service by end of 2027
cards.explain: The law phases down wind and solar credits; projects missing these deadlines lose eligibility.
wrong: Be in service by end of 2035

cards.q: Which clean-energy credits survived longer under the 2025 law?
cards.a: Storage, nuclear and geothermal
cards.explain: Firm and storage resources kept credits longer than wind and solar.

cards.q: Why is 'clean firm power' valued in decarbonization studies?
cards.a: It runs on demand without emissions, cutting system costs
cards.explain: Resources like geothermal, nuclear or gas with capture complement variable renewables and lower total costs.
wrong: It runs only when the sun shines
It is cheaper than all other options always
It replaces the need for any grid

catalyst-with-shayle-kann.summary: Latitude Media's deep-dive show on clean-tech technologies and investing. It explores storage, geothermal, nuclear, data-center power and how new tech gets cheaper.
takeaways: Long-duration storage targets multi-day gaps
Enhanced geothermal borrows oil and gas drilling tech
Small modular reactors aim to cut cost through repetition
Data centers need power faster than the grid can add it

cards.q: What does 'long-duration energy storage' usually mean?
cards.a: Storage lasting beyond about 8-10 hours, up to days
cards.explain: Technologies like iron-air batteries aim to cover longer gaps than typical 2-4 hour lithium batteries.

cards.q: How does enhanced geothermal differ from conventional geothermal?
cards.a: It creates reservoirs in hot rock using drilling and fracturing
cards.explain: Horizontal drilling and stimulation from oil and gas open geothermal to far more locations.

cards.q: What is the pitch for small modular reactors?
cards.a: Factory-built, repeatable units to cut cost and build time
cards.explain: The goal is learning by repetition; costs at scale are still unproven.
wrong: They are already the cheapest power
They run only on solar heat

cards.q: What is the core power challenge for new data centers?
cards.a: Getting large amounts of power connected quickly
cards.explain: 'Speed to power' drives on-site generation, flexible operation and new grid deals.
wrong: Data centers need almost no power
Too much water in the grid
Power is too cheap to sell

cards.q: What does a learning curve (Wright's law) predict?
cards.a: Costs fall by a steady percentage per doubling of production
cards.explain: This pattern explains falling solar, battery and wind costs as deployment grows.
wrong: Costs rise with each new unit built
Costs fall only with new laws

open-circuit.summary: Latitude Media's weekly roundtable on the business news of the energy transition. Common themes include utility bills, load growth, data-center deals, tariffs and project finance.
takeaways: Rising bills often stem from wires, not fuel
Load forecasts include speculative data-center requests
Tariffs and trade rules change project economics
Tax credit transferability reshaped financing

cards.q: Why have many US utility bills been rising?
cards.a: Higher grid infrastructure, capacity and fuel costs
cards.explain: Transmission and distribution spending, wildfire costs, capacity prices and gas prices all push rates up.
wrong: Solar panels are taxed on every bill
Power plants became free to run

cards.q: Why are data-center load forecasts uncertain?
cards.a: Developers file speculative requests in many places
cards.explain: Duplicate interconnection requests can inflate expected demand far above what gets built.
wrong: Data centers use a fixed amount of power
Forecasts are set by federal law
Data centers never connect to the grid

cards.q: What is a large-load tariff?
cards.a: Special terms making big customers cover grid costs and commitments
cards.explain: Utilities require minimum payments or long contracts so other customers are not stuck with stranded costs.
wrong: A discount for any large household
A tax on imported power lines
A fee for small solar systems

cards.q: How do import tariffs affect clean-energy projects?
cards.a: They raise equipment costs, such as solar modules and batteries
cards.explain: Much clean-energy hardware is imported, so tariffs and trade rules shift project costs and timelines.
wrong: They lower costs for all projects
They have no effect on hardware

cards.q: What did tax credit transferability change?
cards.a: Developers can sell clean-energy credits for cash
cards.explain: Created by the IRA, it let projects monetize credits without complex tax equity deals.
wrong: Credits can be used as currency
Credits are paid only to utilities

the-energy-gang.summary: A weekly debate show on energy markets, prices and policy. It covers how power prices are set, battery arbitrage, oil supply and the global gas market.
takeaways: The marginal plant sets wholesale power prices
Prices can go negative when supply floods the grid
Batteries profit from buying low and selling high
US gas prices are increasingly linked to global LNG markets

cards.q: What usually sets the wholesale electricity price at a given hour?
cards.a: The cost of the most expensive plant needed
cards.explain: Under merit-order dispatch the marginal unit, often gas, sets the clearing price.
wrong: The cheapest plant on the grid
A fixed rate set each year

cards.q: Why can wholesale power prices go negative?
cards.a: Supply exceeds demand and some generators still want to run
cards.explain: Inflexible plants and output-based subsidies make some sellers pay to keep generating.

cards.q: How do grid batteries earn money in energy markets?
cards.a: Charging when prices are low and discharging when high
cards.explain: This arbitrage, plus ancillary services, drives rapid storage growth in markets like Texas and California.
wrong: Getting paid only to stay idle

cards.q: What largely drives global oil supply decisions?
cards.a: OPEC+ production choices alongside US shale output
cards.explain: Coordinated output targets from OPEC+ and shale growth heavily shape oil prices.

cards.q: How do LNG exports affect US natural gas prices?
cards.a: They link US prices more closely to global demand
cards.explain: Exporting liquefied gas adds demand and ties domestic markets to international prices.
wrong: They have no effect on prices
They remove all gas from the US

columbia-energy-exchange.summary: Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy covers the policy and geopolitics of energy. Themes include oil markets, energy security, climate diplomacy and critical minerals.
takeaways: Spare capacity gives OPEC+ market power
Europe reshaped gas supply after 2022
Climate finance is central to diplomacy
China dominates mineral processing

cards.q: Why does OPEC+ spare capacity matter for oil markets?
cards.a: It lets producers quickly raise output to ease supply shocks
cards.explain: Spare capacity, mostly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, acts as a buffer and source of market power.

cards.q: How did Europe respond to losing Russian pipeline gas after 2022?
cards.a: Shifted to LNG imports, cut demand and expanded renewables
cards.explain: Europe built LNG import capacity, reduced consumption and accelerated clean energy.
wrong: Switched fully to nuclear in one year

cards.q: What are Brent and WTI?
cards.a: Benchmark crude oil prices
cards.explain: Brent is the main international benchmark; WTI is the US benchmark.

cards.q: What was agreed on climate finance at COP29 in 2024?
cards.a: At least $300 billion per year by 2035 for developing countries
cards.explain: The new finance goal also called for scaling total flows toward $1.3 trillion a year.

cards.q: Why are critical minerals a geopolitical concern?
cards.a: Processing is concentrated, largely in China
cards.explain: China dominates refining of lithium, graphite, rare earths and more, creating supply-chain risk.
wrong: They are only used in jewelry
They are not used in batteries

cleaning-up.summary: Michael Liebreich's long-form interviews with leaders across energy and climate, strong on economics. Recurring ideas include the hydrogen ladder, learning curves, cost of capital and the efficiency of electrification.
takeaways: Use hydrogen where there are few alternatives
Clean tech costs fall with deployment
Cheap capital is crucial for renewables
Electrification needs far less primary energy

cards.q: What does the 'hydrogen ladder' argue?
cards.a: Prioritize hydrogen for uses with few alternatives, not cars or home heat
cards.explain: Fertilizer, refining and some steel rank high; direct electrification usually wins for cars and heating.
wrong: Hydrogen is best for all uses

cards.q: Roughly how much do solar module costs fall with each doubling of production?
cards.a: Roughly 20%
cards.explain: This steady learning rate helps explain the huge drop in solar costs over decades.

cards.q: Why does the cost of capital matter so much for renewables?
cards.a: Most of their cost is upfront, so financing drives price
cards.explain: With no fuel costs, interest rates heavily affect LCOE, especially in developing countries.

cards.q: What is the 'primary energy fallacy'?
cards.a: Assuming clean systems must replace all fossil primary energy
cards.explain: Fossil systems waste much energy as heat, so an electrified system needs far less primary energy.
wrong: Thinking solar uses more fuel than coal

cards.q: How does a cap-and-trade system like the EU ETS work?
cards.a: Caps total emissions and lets firms trade allowances
cards.explain: A declining cap sets a carbon price as companies buy and sell permits.
wrong: Fixes a carbon tax at one price forever

zero.summary: Bloomberg's Akshat Rathi reports on the people and companies racing to net zero. Themes include hard-to-abate sectors like steel and cement, carbon capture, and China's clean-tech manufacturing role.
takeaways: Heavy industry is hard to decarbonize
Green steel can use hydrogen instead of coal
Cement emits CO2 from chemistry, not just fuel
China dominates clean-tech manufacturing

cards.q: Which sectors are called 'hard to abate'?
cards.a: Steel, cement, chemicals, shipping and aviation
cards.explain: They need high heat, chemical processes or dense fuels that are hard to electrify.

cards.q: How can steel be made with far lower emissions?
cards.a: Reducing iron ore with green hydrogen instead of coal
cards.explain: Hydrogen direct reduction plus electric arc furnaces can replace coal-fired blast furnaces.

cards.q: Why is cement hard to decarbonize?
cards.a: Making clinker releases CO2 chemically from limestone
cards.explain: Calcination emits CO2 even with clean heat, so options include alternative materials and capture.
wrong: Cement uses no heat at all

cards.q: What is China's role in clean-tech manufacturing?
cards.a: The largest producer of solar panels, batteries and EVs
cards.explain: China dominates global supply chains, driving down costs worldwide.
wrong: A minor buyer with no factories
A producer of only wind blades

cards.q: What is carbon capture and storage (CCS)?
cards.a: Capturing CO2 from point sources and storing it underground
cards.explain: Applied to industry or power plants, CCS prevents CO2 from reaching the air; costs remain high.

mcj-podcast.summary: My Climate Journey interviews founders and investors building climate tech. It covers how climate startups are financed, where emissions come from and how new markets get created.
takeaways: Energy use is about three-quarters of global emissions
First-of-a-kind projects face a financing gap
The green premium measures clean cost gaps
Advance purchase commitments can create markets

cards.q: Roughly what share of global greenhouse gas emissions come from energy use?
cards.a: About three-quarters
cards.explain: Electricity, heat, transport and industrial fuel use dominate; agriculture and land use make up much of the rest.

cards.q: What is the 'valley of death' for climate hardware?
cards.a: The funding gap between pilot and first commercial plant
cards.explain: First-of-a-kind projects are too big for venture capital and too risky for project finance.
wrong: A desert site for solar farms

cards.q: What is the 'green premium'?
cards.a: The extra cost of a clean option versus the fossil one
cards.explain: Tracking green premiums shows where innovation or policy is needed to make clean options cheaper.
wrong: A bonus paid to green employees

cards.q: How do advance market commitments help carbon removal?
cards.a: Buyers pre-commit to purchase removal, creating demand
cards.explain: Groups like Frontier promise future purchases so startups can scale and lower costs.

cards.q: Why do hardware climate startups need more capital than software ones?
cards.a: They build physical plants with long timelines
cards.explain: Manufacturing, testing and construction are capital intensive and slow to scale.

outrage-optimism.summary: Christiana Figueres and co-hosts discuss global climate politics from the people who helped negotiate the Paris Agreement. It covers how Paris works, COP diplomacy and what 1.5C requires.
takeaways: Paris relies on national pledges that ratchet up
Global stocktakes check progress every five years
1.5C requires roughly halving emissions this decade
COP decisions require consensus

cards.q: How does the Paris Agreement structure national commitments?
cards.a: Countries set their own pledges (NDCs) and strengthen them every five years
cards.explain: Bottom-up nationally determined contributions are meant to ratchet up over time.
wrong: A single global cap enforced by fines
Binding quotas set by the UN

cards.q: What did the first global stocktake at COP28 call for?
cards.a: Transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems
cards.explain: It was the first COP text to address fossil fuels broadly, along with tripling renewables.
wrong: An immediate ban on all coal

cards.q: Roughly what does limiting warming to 1.5C require?
cards.a: Cutting global emissions about in half by 2030 and net zero CO2 around 2050
cards.explain: IPCC pathways show deep cuts this decade and net zero CO2 around mid-century.

cards.q: What was agreed at COP27 in 2022?
cards.a: A fund for loss and damage in vulnerable countries
cards.explain: It addresses climate harms that cannot be adapted to, a long-standing demand of developing nations.

cards.q: How are decisions made at UN climate COPs?
cards.a: By consensus among parties
cards.explain: Any country can block text, which slows progress but gives all parties a voice.

climate-one.summary: The Commonwealth Club's show offers broad conversations on energy, business, justice and culture. It covers climate justice, just transitions, carbon pricing and corporate sustainability.
takeaways: Climate harms fall hardest on those who emit least
Fossil-dependent workers need a just transition
Carbon can be priced by tax or cap-and-trade
The wealthiest emit a disproportionate share

cards.q: What is climate justice?
cards.a: Addressing that those least responsible are often most harmed
cards.explain: Low-income and frontline communities face greater impacts despite lower emissions.

cards.q: What is a 'just transition'?
cards.a: Supporting workers and communities as fossil industries decline
cards.explain: It includes retraining, new investment and protecting pensions in affected regions.
wrong: Moving coal plants to poor areas

cards.q: What are the two main ways to price carbon?
cards.a: A carbon tax or a cap-and-trade system
cards.explain: A tax fixes the price; cap-and-trade fixes the quantity and lets the price float.

cards.q: Roughly what share of global emissions is tied to the richest 10% of people?
cards.a: Roughly half
cards.explain: Studies find consumption by the wealthiest drives a disproportionate share of emissions.

cards.q: What does ESG stand for in corporate sustainability?
cards.a: Environmental, social and governance
cards.explain: ESG frameworks assess companies on climate, labor, governance and related risks.

the-energy-transition-show.summary: Chris Nelder's technical deep dives on energy markets, grids and resources. Topics include ancillary services, energy-only markets, nodal pricing, EROI and the move from baseload to flexibility.
takeaways: Grids buy more than energy: reserves and regulation too
Energy-only markets rely on scarcity price spikes
Nodal prices reflect congestion and losses
High-renewable grids need flexibility, not baseload

cards.q: What are ancillary services?
cards.a: Grid services like frequency regulation and reserves
cards.explain: They keep the grid stable and are bought separately from bulk energy.

cards.q: How does an energy-only market like ERCOT reward new capacity?
cards.a: Through high scarcity price spikes instead of capacity payments
cards.explain: Prices can spike to thousands of dollars per MWh during shortages, signaling investment.

cards.q: What is locational marginal pricing?
cards.a: Prices that vary by grid location due to congestion and losses
cards.explain: Nodal prices signal where power is scarce and where new resources or lines are most valuable.
wrong: Prices that vary by customer income

cards.q: What is EROI?
cards.a: Energy return on investment: energy delivered per unit invested
cards.explain: It compares how much usable energy a source delivers relative to the energy needed to produce it.

cards.q: Why are high-renewable grids shifting from 'baseload' to 'flexibility'?
cards.a: Variable supply needs resources that ramp up and down
cards.explain: Batteries, demand response and flexible plants fit around wind and solar better than inflexible plants.

concepts.summary: Core vocabulary and mental models for energy and sustainability professionals.
takeaways: kW is power, kWh is energy
The marginal plant, often gas, sets power prices
Scope 3 is usually the biggest share of corporate emissions
Removals and additional PPAs are stronger claims than offsets and unbundled RECs

cards.q: What is the difference between kW and kWh?
cards.a: kW is power (rate); kWh is energy (amount)
cards.explain: A 1 kW heater running for 3 hours uses 3 kWh; bills charge per kWh.
wrong: kW is energy; kWh is power

cards.q: What is capacity factor?
cards.a: Actual output divided by maximum possible output over time
cards.explain: US solar is roughly 20-25%, onshore wind 30-40%, nuclear above 90%.
wrong: Peak output divided by average demand
Share of time a plant is under repair
Plant size divided by land area

cards.q: What is LCOE?
cards.a: Lifetime cost per MWh of electricity from a plant
cards.explain: Levelized cost of energy spreads capital, fuel and operating costs over lifetime output.
wrong: The retail price on a customer bill
The fuel cost of one hour

cards.q: On unsubsidized LCOE, how do new utility solar and onshore wind compare with new gas?
cards.a: Generally among the cheapest new sources
cards.explain: They are typically at or below new gas, though they are variable and need firming.

cards.q: What is a PPA?
cards.a: A long-term contract to buy power at a set price
cards.explain: Power purchase agreements are how corporations buy renewable power and help projects get financed.
wrong: A government ban on fossil plants
A one-time power purchase at spot prices

cards.q: What is the merit order?
cards.a: Dispatching plants from cheapest to most expensive
cards.explain: The last plant needed sets the wholesale price for that period.
wrong: Paying all plants the same fixed price

cards.q: Why does natural gas often set electricity prices?
cards.a: Gas plants are frequently the marginal plant
cards.explain: Since the marginal plant sets the price, gas fuel costs pass through to wholesale power prices.
wrong: Gas is always the cheapest fuel
Laws fix power prices to gas

cards.q: What is the duck curve?
cards.a: Net demand dips midday with solar, then ramps steeply at sunset
cards.explain: Abundant midday solar lowers net load, followed by a sharp evening ramp; batteries help shift solar into the evening.
wrong: Demand peaking at noon every day

cards.q: What is curtailment?
cards.a: Deliberately reducing renewable output the grid cannot use
cards.explain: It happens with oversupply or transmission congestion; storage and transmission reduce it.
wrong: Cutting power to customers in heat waves

cards.q: Why can wholesale power prices turn negative?
cards.a: Supply exceeds demand and some generators keep running
cards.explain: Inflexible plants and output-based incentives make some sellers pay to keep producing.

cards.q: What does a capacity market pay for?
cards.a: Availability to supply power in future years
cards.explain: Operators like PJM pay resources to be available; recent PJM auctions cleared at record prices as demand grew.

cards.q: What is an interconnection queue?
cards.a: The waiting line to connect new projects to the grid
cards.explain: Often years long, it is a major bottleneck for new renewables and storage.
wrong: A line at a utility office
A list of customers awaiting meters

cards.q: What are Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions?
cards.a: Direct, purchased energy, and value-chain emissions
cards.explain: Scope 1 is direct; Scope 2 is purchased electricity and heat; Scope 3 is everything else in the value chain.

cards.q: Which scope is usually the largest share of a company's footprint?
cards.a: Scope 3
cards.explain: Value-chain emissions from suppliers and product use usually dwarf direct operations.

cards.q: What is CO2e?
cards.a: Greenhouse gases converted to a CO2 equivalent using GWP
cards.explain: Global warming potential weights each gas by its warming effect relative to CO2.

cards.q: How does methane's GWP differ over 20 vs 100 years?
cards.a: Over 80x CO2 over 20 years; about 28-30x over 100
cards.explain: Methane is potent but short-lived, so its impact looks larger over shorter timeframes.

cards.q: How does net zero (per SBTi) differ from carbon neutral?
cards.a: Net zero cuts about 90% and removes the rest
cards.explain: 'Carbon neutral' claims often rely mainly on buying offsets rather than deep reductions.
wrong: They mean exactly the same thing
Net zero relies only on offsets

cards.q: What is the difference between avoidance offsets and removals?
cards.a: Avoidance prevents emissions; removals pull CO2 from the air
cards.explain: Removals (forests, direct air capture, enhanced weathering) are generally higher quality and pricier.
wrong: Avoidance pulls CO2 from the air

cards.q: What is a REC?
cards.a: A certificate for 1 MWh of renewable generation
cards.explain: Renewable energy certificates track the environmental attributes of clean power.
wrong: A permit for 1 ton of CO2

cards.q: Why is additionality important for clean-energy claims?
cards.a: A strong claim causes new clean energy that otherwise would not exist
cards.explain: Unbundled RECs from existing plants are weak claims; PPAs that finance new projects are stronger.

cards.q: What does a heat pump COP of 3 mean?
cards.a: 3 units of heat per unit of electricity
cards.explain: Modern heat pumps reach roughly 2.5-4, versus about 95% efficiency for a good gas furnace.
wrong: 3 times less heat than a furnace

cards.q: What is energy intensity?
cards.a: Energy used per unit of output, such as GDP
cards.explain: Falling energy intensity shows efficiency gains in the data.
wrong: Total energy used by a country

cards.q: What are SDG 7 and SDG 13?
cards.a: Affordable and clean energy, and climate action
cards.explain: They are two of the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals for 2015-2030.
wrong: Clean water and life on land

cards.q: What are the Paris Agreement temperature goals?
cards.a: Well below 2C, pursuing 1.5C
cards.explain: Measured relative to pre-industrial levels; adopted in 2015.

cards.q: What does the SBTi do?
cards.a: Validates company emissions targets against climate science
cards.explain: The Science Based Targets initiative checks targets align with Paris goals and sets a net-zero standard.

cards.q: What duration do most grid-scale lithium batteries provide?
cards.a: Typically 2-4 hours
cards.explain: They suit daily shifting such as moving solar to the evening peak; longer durations need other tech.

cards.q: What is a virtual power plant?
cards.a: Aggregated distributed devices acting like one power plant
cards.explain: Batteries, EVs, thermostats and solar can be coordinated to supply power or cut demand on command.
wrong: A power plant simulated in software
A plant run by remote robots

cards.q: What is demand response?
cards.a: Customers reducing or shifting use when the grid is strained
cards.explain: Paid or price-driven reductions lower peaks and can avoid building peaking plants.
wrong: Building plants to meet all demand

cards.q: Why is data-center growth reshaping power planning?
cards.a: It drives fast load growth after years of flat demand
cards.explain: AI and cloud loads are large and concentrated, straining generation, transmission and capacity markets.

cards.q: Under the July 2025 US law, when must wind and solar qualify for tax credits?
cards.a: Begin construction by July 4, 2026, or be in service by end of 2027
cards.explain: The law phases down wind and solar credits; storage, nuclear and geothermal credits last longer.
wrong: Be in service by end of 2030
